title: The elder
hook: Orthodox Christians seek a spiritual father or mother for guidance

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chotki: a rope of wool, a prayer at every knot. Your line was a knot, a prayer. Where did your hand find the string? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

Night, in the temple of the Lord. A boy named Samuel, who serves there, hears his name called, and runs to the old priest Eli. Here I am, he says. Eli says, I didn't call you. Go back and lie down. It happens again. And again. Eli is old, his eyes growing dim, but he's the one who works out what's going on. The Lord is calling the boy. So Eli tells him what to say if it comes once more: "Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth." Eli doesn't hear the voice himself. He helps someone else hear it. That is the picture behind today's word, from the Russian Orthodox tradition: starets. The elder.

Starets, in Russian, simply means an old man. But the role isn't really about age. An elder is a monk, sometimes a nun, now and then a lay person, known for prayer and for seeing clearly into hearts, whom other people seek out for guidance. A woman in the role is a staritsa. In Greek the elder is a geron. Tradition traces the role back to the desert. People would walk out to an old monk's cell and say, in substance, Abba, give me a word. Not a lecture. A word: one sentence to live on for a while. Abba means father; a woman teacher was called amma, mother. Why would anyone need this? Because everything this week has a weak spot. Watchfulness, tears and the prayer rope can all be bent by the one doing them. A mind can mistake its own pride for holiness, and never notice. Proverbs puts it plainly: "Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety." The elder is a second pair of eyes on the soul. The novelist Dostoevsky put an elder at the heart of The Brothers Karamazov, Father Zosima, and described the bond as freely handing your will to someone wiser, for the sake of becoming free. That's the strong form, and it's a long, trusted relationship, not advice on demand. In everyday Orthodox life, this guidance can come through a priest who hears confession and becomes a spiritual father. Other churches use other names: Catholics speak of spiritual direction, and some Protestants of a mentor or a pastor.

Here's the practice: ask someone wise for guidance. Sit, and let one question rise, something you've been deciding on your own. Then let a face come to mind: someone you trust who sees more clearly than you on this. A grandparent, a pastor, an old friend, a teacher. Imagine asking them. What might they see that you can't? If you pray, you can say Samuel's line: Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth. Then plan to really ask them, today. The bell holds the time.
Starets. The elder: someone seasoned in prayer whom others seek out for guidance, a second pair of eyes on the soul.
Your line: go to the elder. Today, take one real question to someone wiser than you, and hear the whole answer before you reply. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians seek guidance from a spiritual father or mother, who may be the priest who hears their confession; some travel to monasteries to ask a recognized elder for a word.

notes: The index hook says 'many Orthodox seek...'; the spoken script avoids the count ('whom other people seek out'). The hook field is softened to 'Orthodox Christians seek...' for the claims rule; the outline line still says 'many'.
staritsa (старица) for a female elder and γέρων / gerontissa: confirm terms. Only 'staritsa' and 'geron' are spoken.
'Abba, give me a word' is the common form of the request in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers; paraphrased. 'amma' for women teachers (e.g. Amma Syncletica) not named.

Dostoevsky's description of an elder (Book 1, ch. 5) paraphrased: taking your will into his and submitting freely, for the sake of freedom. Garnett's 1912 translation is public domain but not on the validator list, so no quotation.
'In everyday Orthodox life, this guidance can come through a priest who hears confession' is a general description; confirm or soften.
1 Samuel 3:2–8 paraphrased (Eli's dim eyes; the boy called again and again).
Editor pass: 'the roots go back to the desert' (an unsourced historical claim) softened to 'tradition traces the role back to the desert'.
